What we confirmed on official pages

  • Tax Help page offers online appeal of values (Appealing Tax Values); per FAQ, personal property appeals within 30 days of bill date
  • 2026 bill due Sept 1, 2026; pay without interest through Jan 5, 2027; interest begins Jan 6, 2027
  • Checks payable to County of Carteret; mail to PO Box 96264, Charlotte, NC 28296-6264
  • Partial payments allowed; hardship payment arrangement application available
  • Individual/business personal property appeals must be submitted within 30 days of bill date (online via Tax Help page)

Tax rate

Selling in Carteret County?
We buy Carteret County houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

What we could not confirm

  • E-recording on Carteret page

Carteret County by the numbers

Which Carteret County office handles property tax?

Carteret County runs assessing and collecting out of a single Tax Administration office, led by an appointed Tax Administrator. The commissioners make the appointment, and the administrator also reports on legal compliance to state bodies in Raleigh.

Walk-in service is on the first floor of the Administration Building, 302 Courthouse Square in Beaufort, and at a Western Office on Cedar Point Blvd. in Cedar Point (701 Cedar Point Blvd., NC 28584). The phone is 252-728-8485, and weekday hours at both are 8 a.m. to 5 p.m., holidays excepted. Office staff also serve the review board that hears value appeals.

Its stated job covers appraisal, assessment, billing and collection of tax on real, business and personal property, plus keeping the records the state Department of Revenue asks for. A seller can ask this office what is owed on a parcel and whether a relief claim is on file.

When are Carteret County property taxes due?

The bill falls due on September 1, but interest does not begin until January 6 of the next year. From then the county charges 2% for January and 0.75% for each later month.

EventDate or ruleSource
Annual bills mailedAugust 2026 mailing covered more than 82,000 billsCarteret County news release
Taxes dueSeptember 1G.S. 105-360 and county
Last day without interestJanuary 5County delinquent taxes page
Interest starts2% for January, then 0.75% a monthCounty and G.S. 105-360
Personal property value appeal window30 days counted from the bill dateCounty Appealing Tax Values page
Delinquent lien advertisementPublished between March 1 and June 30County delinquent taxes page

The county's August 2026 release puts the fiscal year 2026-27 rate at 22.5 cents per $100 of assessed value. Real and personal property get separate bills. Property in Beaufort, Bogue, Cape Carteret, Cedar Point, Emerald Isle, Morehead City or Peletier receives a single bill with county and town tax combined. A mailed check is credited as of its postmark.

How do I appeal a Carteret County assessed value?

Submit the Real Property Appeal Form to the Tax Administration Office within the window on your value notice. For a reappraisal notice the county sets that window at 30 days from the notice date, and it limits appeals to the assessed value, ruling out arguments about the rate or the bill.

The county's last general reappraisal used a January 1, 2025 market value, and its notice tells owners to compare their property's characteristics and comparable sales against what was used. The assessor is presumed to have acted in good faith, so the burden sits with the owner. Evidence that helps: sales of similar nearby homes, damage photos and repair quotes.

  • First level: the Board of Equalization and Review, nine local residents counting two alternates, which mails its Notice of Decision within a month of meeting.
  • Second level: the state Property Tax Commission, which you reach by filing within 30 days of that notice. Hearings are typically in Raleigh, and a lawyer may be needed.
  • Third level: the North Carolina Court of Appeals, only on a question of law, and then the state Supreme Court.

Boats, aircraft, mobile homes and business equipment follow a different path: file within 30 days of the date on the annual bill, and the county sets a conference before issuing a final decision. The result can go down, up or stay put, and it applies only from that year onward. Statewide, G.S. 105-290 sets the 30-day window to reach the Property Tax Commission.

What property tax relief can a Carteret County owner claim?

North Carolina offers three ways to cut a home's bill, and an owner can take only one. The county tax office takes the application, not the state.

  • Age or disability: the owner must be 65 or older, or permanently and totally disabled, with 2026 income no higher than $38,800. A qualifying owner has the larger of $25,000 or half the value taken off the taxable base.
  • Veteran exclusion: $45,000 of appraised value comes off for a qualifying disabled veteran or unmarried surviving spouse, and the state form lists no age or income test.
  • Circuit breaker: the cap on the bill is 4.0% of income, rising to 5.0% for incomes above $38,800 and up to $58,200. Five years of owning and living in the home come first, and the excess tax is deferred rather than forgiven.

The application is Form AV-9. File it during the January listing period if you can, because the assessor must accept it until June 1. A circuit breaker claim must be renewed yearly, and a sale, a death or a move triggers repayment of the deferred amounts for the three prior years. Carteret's delinquent tax page steers older, disabled and veteran owners toward these programs. Read the statutes at G.S. 105-277.1, 105-277.1B and 105-277.1C.

How can I pay a Carteret County tax bill?

Four routes work: the web portal, the phone line, the mail and the counter. The portal accepts cards, eCheck and PayPal, while 1-888-544-9433 takes card payments if you have the bill in hand.

  • Mail: a check payable to County of Carteret, sent to PO Box 96264, Charlotte, NC 28296-6264.
  • Counter: Beaufort or Cedar Point, paying by cash, check, money order or card.
  • Drop box: at the courthouse entrance, no cash, processed the next business day.

Fees apply to cards. The county's payment page prints a $1.50 flat charge for an eCheck and 2.50% plus $0.30 a transaction on credit cards. Partial payments in any amount are allowed online, but the full balance must be in before delinquency, and the county's news release says the phone line does not take partial amounts. An owner who cannot pay in full can apply for a hardship payment arrangement. Interest keeps running under it, but it may lower the odds of garnishment or foreclosure.

What happens when Carteret County taxes go unpaid?

The lien on the parcel stays, interest keeps growing, and the county can use enforcement tools. G.S. 105-355 fixes the lien to the parcel as of the listing date, with penalties, interest and costs riding along.

The county lists wage and bank garnishment, state income tax refund setoff, setoff against lottery winnings, attachment of rent, seizure and sale of personal property, and foreclosure on real property. The foreclosure route, in G.S. 105-374, resembles a mortgage foreclosure and ends at an auction on the courthouse steps, followed by a commissioner's report and a ten-day window for higher bids. Redemption stays open until confirmation, at the price of the taxes, penalties, interest and costs.

A sale before that point is usually cleaner. According to the county, the advertisement of a delinquent account starts the advanced foreclosure process, so an owner who is behind should call 252-728-8485 before the March 1 to June 30 publication period.

How does a sale affect a Carteret County tax bill?

A tax balance follows the parcel as a lien, so it is normally cleared at closing. Request a current figure from the Tax Administration Office, and agree with the closing attorney how this year's bill is divided.

Filing the deed is a separate errand at the register of deeds, covered on our Carteret County register of deeds page. If a circuit breaker deferral is on the property, the deferred taxes for the preceding three years become due on a transfer.

Census QuickFacts puts Carteret County at 70,469 residents on July 1, 2025, with 54,293 housing units. Across 2020-2024 the median owned home was valued at $333,300, 74.7% of units were owner-occupied, and 30.1% of residents were 65 or older. The data is on the Census Bureau page for Carteret County.

More questions about Carteret County, NC Property Tax Guide

What is the Carteret County property tax rate?

The 2026-27 county rate is 22.5 cents per $100, per the county's August 2026 release. Parcels inside a town add the town rate and arrive on one combined bill.

When do Carteret County taxes become delinquent?

On January 6, following the September 1 due date. A payment through January 5 owes no interest; after that comes 2% for January and 0.75% for each month beyond.

What is the deadline to contest a Carteret County assessment?

Real property owners have thirty days from the change of value notice, and personal property owners have thirty days from the bill date. Only value is open to challenge.

Where do I pay my Carteret County tax bill in person?

Visit the Beaufort office or the Western Office in Cedar Point, both open weekdays from 8 a.m. until 5 p.m. A drop box at the courthouse entrance accepts checks.

Can Carteret County set up a payment plan?

Yes, in limited cases. The county offers a hardship payment arrangement by application and lets owners pay in partial amounts before delinquency. A plan does not stop interest from running.

Selling in Caswell County?

Which office handles property tax in Caswell County?

The Caswell County Tax Office handles listings, exemption forms and bill payment, and it works from the courthouse at 139 E. Church Street in Yanceyville. Mail goes to PO Box 204, Yanceyville, NC 27379, the phone line is (336) 694-4194 ext. 5116, and the county directory lists weekday hours of eight to five.

The same directory entry explains how to pay a bill by card through an outside payment service. A fee applies, and it rises as the tax amount rises. Bill numbers begin with R for real estate or P for personal property, and you leave off the zero that follows the letter when you type the number in. The county home page also carries a Pay A Tax Bill link to an online bill search.

Two other offices matter to a seller. The Register of Deeds sits downstairs in the same courthouse complex and answers at (336) 694-4197. The county GIS office, on (336) 694-4194 ext. 115, matches parcels to maps. With a bill still open, call the tax office first for a payoff on the parcel.

What are the Caswell County property tax rate and revaluation dates?

Caswell County set its rate at 62.7 cents per $100 of value for property listed as of January 1, 2025, and the county was last reappraised effective January 1, 2024. The state schedule shows the next countywide reappraisal for 2028. The table gathers the figures exactly as the official documents print them.

Which one covers your house depends on the parcel, so ask the tax office when you want the exact combined charge for an address. For its rate-setting estimate the ordinance used $2,161,354,092 of real, personal and public service property and a 99.04 percent collection rate.

For the current year's rate, call the tax office or open the adopted budget ordinance on the county home page.

How does a Caswell County owner appeal an assessment?

Value disputes go to the county's board of equalization and review, so begin by asking the tax office for the board's meeting dates and appeal form ahead of the spring session. The outline of the calendar comes from state law and is the same here as elsewhere:

  • The board's opening session lands somewhere from the first April Monday to the first May Monday.
  • Outside a reappraisal year the board wraps up about three Mondays after opening and generally stops by July 1. In a reappraisal year it has until December 1.
  • Request a hearing before adjournment, either in writing or by showing up. A decision notice mailed late in the session extends your window by 15 days from the mailing.
  • Its written decision is mailed within 30 days after it adjourns.
  • Still unhappy? Put a written notice of appeal to the Property Tax Commission in the mail within 30 days of the board's decision date, copying the county assessor.

The 2024 reappraisal is the latest, which ties the next large wave of appeals to 2028. In between, a value usually moves only after a physical change to the property, a clerical error or a change in permitted use, so a quiet-year appeal should name one of those.

The state's January 1, 2025 sales ratio study printed a median ratio of 104.97 for Caswell County. If your value looks high, gather recent nearby sales of comparable houses and dated photos of defects present on January 1.

Which property tax breaks can a Caswell County homeowner claim?

Three state homestead programs exist, and an owner can draw on just one. Applications use Form AV-9 and go to the county tax office. The county has to accept them up to June 1 before the tax year.

  • Elderly or disabled exclusion: shelters half of a home's appraised value or $25,000, whichever is larger, for an owner who is 65 or older or totally and permanently disabled and whose prior-year income fits under the cap. The 2026 cap printed by NCDOR is $38,800.
  • Disabled veteran exclusion: waives $45,000 of appraised value whatever the applicant's age or income. Form NCDVA-9 is filled out with a Veterans Service Officer first.
  • Circuit breaker deferment: caps the bill at 4 percent of income for owners under the cap and 5 percent for those up to 150 percent of it ($58,200 for 2026), and the owner reapplies every year.

Sellers should know the circuit breaker's catch: the deferred amount is a lien, and a transfer makes the previous three fiscal years' deferrals payable. A house that used the deferment therefore carries an extra payoff on the closing statement.

The Caswell tax office page links the state's exemption, exclusion and present-use value forms, as well as business personal property listing forms.

How is the Caswell County tax bill handled at a sale?

The tax stays with the land, so an open balance is paid out of the sale at closing. The statutory lien for a given year takes hold on January 1, the listing date, along with later penalties, interest and costs.

A bill is due September 1 and costs face value until January 6. Interest then begins at 2 percent for the balance of January, followed by three-fourths of a percent for each month or part of one. A seller whose prior-year bill is open takes those charges to the closing table.

The deed adds its own charges. The transferor pays the state's conveyance excise tax, $1.00 per $500 of price or fraction, to the register of deeds ahead of recording, and statute fixes the recording fees ($26 for an ordinary instrument's first 15 pages, $64 for a deed of trust's first 35).

If a bill stays unpaid for long, the county may sue to foreclose the tax lien the way a lender would foreclose a mortgage, and the parcel goes to auction at the courthouse door. Redemption stays open until confirmation, on payment of what is owed.

What should a seller know about Caswell County itself?

Caswell County is thinly settled, with 53.5 people per square mile in 2020. Yanceyville is where the courthouse sits, and Milton is the other town named on the county website. The Census Bureau counts 22,563 residents in its July 1, 2025 estimate, down 0.8 percent from the 2020 base, across about 425 square miles of land.

Homes are inexpensive here: the Census lists a $164,500 median for owned homes in 2020-2024, with owners living in 75.2 percent of them. Median household income comes to $59,755, and a quarter of residents (25.4 percent) are 65 or older, an age group the elderly exclusion is built for.

Workers average a 30.6-minute trip to their jobs. The county markets two industrial sites, the Pelham Business Park and the Yanceyville Business Park, and Piedmont Community College offers workforce training. County Environmental Health handles private septic permits, so a seller with a septic system can ask that office for the records on file.

More questions about Caswell County, NC Property Tax Guide

Which number reaches the Caswell County tax office?

Phone the tax office on (336) 694-4194 ext. 5116. The county directory puts it at 139 E. Church Street in Yanceyville, open Monday through Friday, eight to five. Keep your bill number handy and drop the zero after the R or P.

What is the Caswell County property tax rate?

The 2025-26 budget ordinance levied 62.7 cents on each $100 of property listed as of January 1, 2025. The same ordinance added 3.3 cents of fire district tax in the Casville and County Fire Service districts and set solid waste fees of $55 and $75. For the current year, ask the tax office.

When is the next Caswell County revaluation?

The state schedule shows 2028, following the reappraisal effective January 1, 2024. Counties must reappraise at least every eighth year and may choose shorter cycles. Confirm the date with the tax office, since schedules can move.

When are Caswell County property taxes due?

September 1 is the due date. Paying before January 6 of the next year costs face value, and from that day interest starts at 2 percent, moving to three-fourths of a percent monthly. A mailed payment counts on its postmark date.

Is a sale possible with Caswell County tax still owed?

Yes. Whatever is open, interest included, comes out of your proceeds at the closing table. Request a payoff figure from the tax office before choosing a closing date, and ask if a circuit breaker deferral adds a second balance.

Catawba County by the numbers

Which office runs property tax in Catawba County?

The Catawba County Tax Office lists, appraises and assesses all real and personal property in the county, and it also collects the county's taxes. Its page gives (828) 465-8414 for general questions, and a separate line, (828) 465-8436, for tax relief appointments. Mail for relief applications goes to Assessor's Office, Attn: Tax Relief, Box 368, Newton, NC 28658-0368.

The county reports a fiscal year 2025 tax base of $31,422,508,337, a levy of $125,365,125 and a collection rate of 98.57 percent. The tax office has also earned the Certificate of Excellence in Assessment Administration from the International Association of Assessing Officers, which the county says makes it the fourth jurisdiction in North Carolina to hold it.

Apple Inc. is the largest taxpayer on the county's list at 4.70 percent of taxable assessed value, followed by Duke Energy Carolinas at 3.37 percent. The ten largest taxpayers together account for 12.15 percent. Your own bill depends on your parcel's value, the county rate and the fire district or town where the parcel sits.

What do the Catawba County fire district and town rates add up to?

The county rate is .3985 per $100 of assessed value, and every parcel also pays either a fire district tax or a municipal tax. The county tax page prints the full list, and the table shows the main figures exactly as printed.

When is the Catawba County revaluation, and how do appeals work?

Catawba County revalues every four years, current values took effect January 1, 2023, and the next countywide revaluation takes effect January 1, 2027. State law only requires a revaluation every eight years, so the county's four-year rhythm is shorter than the minimum. The county says staff are analyzing sales and market trends for the 2027 round.

The tax page states that the Board of Equalization and Review has adjourned for new appeals in the current tax year and that the next opportunity to appeal is January 2027. That lines up with the notices that follow a revaluation. The path starts with an informal review and moves up only if that fails:

  • When notices of value are mailed, ask the tax office how to request an informal review of your value, and use the form that comes with the notice.
  • When informal review fails, take the case to the county board of equalization and review, asking for a hearing in writing or in person before adjournment.
  • The state Property Tax Commission is the next stop, reached by written notice filed within 30 days after the board mails its ruling.

The county's revaluation page explains that revaluation updates values, not rates. Elected boards adopt the rate in the annual budget ordinance, which the county says is typically finalized in June. An appeal can reduce your value but cannot change the rate.

Which property tax relief programs does Catawba County offer?

The county tax relief page lists four programs: the elderly or disabled homestead exclusion, the disabled veteran exclusion, the circuit breaker deferment, and the AV-10 application for other exclusions. An owner may pick only one of the first three.

  • Elderly or disabled exclusion: open to owners who were 65 or disabled on January 1, own the home, live in the county and report income under the printed limit. The state formula takes off $25,000 or half the appraised value, whichever is greater. A 65-plus applicant skips the disability certificate, and approval carries forward until you move, sell, rent, change the deed or see income pass the limit.
  • Disabled veteran exclusion: removes up to $45,000 of assessed value from the permanent residence, with no income test. The county wants discharge papers plus VA certification of permanent, total, service-connected disability, or proof of specially adapted housing benefits.
  • Circuit breaker deferment: holds the bill to 4 or 5 percent of income for owners who have lived in and owned the home five years or more. The deferred part is a lien, repayable with interest for the current year and three earlier ones once the property transfers.

June 1 is the yearly cutoff for all three, and the circuit breaker needs a new application every year. The AV-10 for religious, charitable, historic and similar exclusions is filed in January. NCDOR printed $38,800 as the 2026 income limit, with $58,200 as the 150 percent mark for the circuit breaker.

How is Catawba County tax settled when a house sells?

The sale proceeds clear whatever tax is open. A year's lien attaches on the January 1 listing date, and the bill falls due September 1. Because every parcel pays county tax plus a fire or town levy, a Hickory payoff will not match one for a house in a rural fire district.

Interest is absent through January 5, then runs at 2 percent for the rest of January and three-fourths of a percent per month beyond.

Circuit breaker owners get the surprise: transferring the property is a disqualifying event, so the deferred amounts become payable at the sale. Ask the tax office for a statement showing the current bill and any deferred balance.

Deed charges are handled with the Register of Deeds, a separate office; the seller pays the state excise tax there before the deed records.

What does Catawba County look like for a house seller?

Catawba County sits in the western foothills of the Blue Ridge, covers 413 square miles, and was formed from Lincoln County in 1842. County offices use Newton addresses, and Hickory, Conover, Claremont, Maiden, Long View, Catawba and Brookford are the other municipalities on the county's tax page.

The Census Bureau's July 1, 2025 estimate shows 170,172 residents, a 5.9 percent gain on the 2020 base, in 77,827 housing units. Owners hold 72.2 percent of homes, the 2020-2024 median home value is $241,600, and gross rent has a median of $965. Builders pulled 1,944 permits in 2025, and the median household earns $67,864.

Manufacturing and cable, gear and tape plants show up in the largest-taxpayer list, and the mean commute is 23.4 minutes. For comparison, the 2025-26 state rate table lists .3985 for Catawba County and .6270 for Caswell County.

More questions about Catawba County, NC Property Tax Guide

What is the Catawba County property tax rate?

The county's own tax page prints .3985 per $100. Each parcel adds either a fire district rate or a town or city rate (.46 in Hickory, .45 in Newton, for instance), and the two together make the combined rate.

When do Catawba County property values change next?

The next countywide revaluation takes effect January 1, 2027, after the one that took effect January 1, 2023. Catawba County revalues every four years. Appeals for the new values open once notices are mailed.

Which phone line handles Catawba County tax relief?

Call (828) 465-8436 to book an appointment about tax relief, or (828) 465-8414 for general tax office questions. Relief applications can be mailed to Assessor's Office, Attn: Tax Relief, Box 368, Newton, NC 28658-0368. The deadline for the homestead programs is June 1.

Do I have to pay off deferred circuit breaker taxes when I sell?

Yes. Selling ends the deferment, and the deferred amounts for this year and the three before it become payable with interest. Get the deferred balance from the tax office ahead of closing so it can be paid from the proceeds.

Is a disabled veteran exclusion available in Catawba County?

Yes. It excludes up to $45,000 of assessed value of a permanent residence and has no income limit. The veteran needs discharge proof plus VA certification of permanent and total service-connected disability, and the application is due by June 1.

Chatham County by the numbers

Which Chatham County office does what on property tax?

Chatham County splits the work between a Listing Division, an Appraisal Division and a Collections Division, all under Tax Administration. The Listing Division sits at 12 East Street in Pittsboro, ground floor of the government annex facing the Pittsboro traffic circle, and its public counter operates on weekdays, eight to five. Correspondence goes to PO Box 908 in Pittsboro (ZIP 27312), and the listing line is 919-542-8250.

Questions about what your house is worth on the tax roll go to the Appraisal Division at 919-542-8211. The county states the mission as fair, accurate valuation of real and personal property across Chatham. Bills, payments and returned-check issues go through Collections.

Census QuickFacts counts 85,111 people in Chatham for mid-2025, 11.6% more than in 2020, spread over 681.68 land square miles: see Census QuickFacts. Pittsboro, Siler City and Goldston levy their own town taxes, and slices of Chatham near Cary and Apex are billed for those towns too. That mix is why two Chatham neighbors can have different bills on similar houses.

How often does Chatham County reappraise real estate?

Chatham reappraises every four years, which is tighter than the eight-year ceiling North Carolina sets for every county under G.S. 105-286. The most recent reappraisal took effect on January 1, 2025, and the one before it was in 2021. If the county keeps that rhythm, the next value date lands in 2029, though the Appraisal Division is the office to confirm that with.

For the 2025 round, county appraisers studied recorded sales, building cost data and income and expense figures from commercial property to estimate values for more than 48,000 parcels. Notices went out by mail in March 2025. Many parts of the county went up in value from 2021, a few went down and some stayed about the same.

The tax rate is a separate step. The county explained then that bills stay unknowable until each taxing body adopts a rate from its budget. In the budget approved for fiscal year 2026-27, commissioners kept the county rate at 60 cents per $100 of valuation after the revaluation year, as the county's budget announcement put it.

What are the 2026 property tax rates in Chatham County?

The county-only rate is 0.60, and every other district adds its own piece on top, according to the county's 2026 rate sheet. The sheet prints a district rate and a combined rate for each area, so the combined figure is the one that matches a bill. A few lines from that sheet are below.

The same sheet lists fire and sanitary districts such as Bonlee, Moncure, North Chatham and Northview, plus solid waste fees for Pittsboro and Goldston and vehicle fees for Pittsboro, Siler City, Cary and Apex. The county budget year begins July 1, which is also when commissioners and the towns fix rates. A call to the tax office will tell you which district covers a given street address.

What is the path for contesting a Chatham County value?

Begin with the county's comparison tool, file with the Appraisal Division next, and take the matter to the county's equalization board only if the staff review leaves you unsatisfied. During the 2025 reappraisal the county urged owners to test their notice against nearby sales on its Comper website. An online appeal form lives on the appraisal page, and a printable paper form is available too.

  • Comparable sales, from your own research, the county's site or a real estate professional.
  • Photos of the inside and outside of the property, showing condition and upgrades.
  • A recent fee appraisal, such as one done for a purchase or refinance.

After an appeal is received, a tax office representative contacts the owner to go over the value. Still unresolved? Request a hearing, and the board mails its written finding. The 2025 appeal window shut on May 19, 2025 at five in the afternoon. For 2026 the board began April 6 and adjourned April 20, and it took no new appeals after adjourning.

Two statutes set the outer frame. G.S. 105-322 puts the board's first sitting in April or early May, and G.S. 105-290 gives a 30-day clock for taking a loss to the Property Tax Commission.

Which Chatham County relief programs reduce a tax bill?

Chatham runs three state programs plus one local grant. The state-program applications must reach the Tax Listing Office before June 1 of the year you qualify, and the county page lists the following.

  • Elderly or disabled exclusion: $25,000 or half the residence's appraised value, whichever is larger, for residents of 65 or more, or with a total and permanent disability, whose income does not exceed $38,800.
  • Disabled veteran exclusion: $45,000 off the appraised value, for a resident who is a disabled veteran or an unmarried surviving spouse; the NCDVA-9 form comes from the NC Division of Veterans Affairs.
  • Circuit breaker deferment: taxes capped at a share of income for 65-plus or totally disabled owners with income at or under $58,200 and five calendar years of owning and living in the house. Excess tax stays as a lien, and the latest three years of deferred tax come due with interest on a disqualifying event. A new application is needed each year.
  • Low Income Tax Relief Program: up to $500, never more than 50% of the current bill, for residents with five years of ownership and residence in the home and household income at or below 60% of area median income. Households receiving Food and Nutrition Services skip the income paperwork.

Disability claims require a certificate from a North Carolina physician or a government agency. Heirs or executors must tell the office when a recipient dies, and a surviving spouse reapplies for the following year. Failing to report a disqualifying event means recovery of the exclusion plus penalties and interest.

What are the due dates, and what if tax is still owed at closing?

Payment is due each September 1 and carries no interest through January 5, under G.S. 105-360. Interest of 2% begins January 6, and from February 1 it adds three-fourths of one percent for every month or fraction. A check or electronic payment that bounces draws a penalty of $25 or 10% of the payment, whichever is greater, up to $1,000, according to the Collections Division page.

A tax lien attaches on the listing date under G.S. 105-355, so the bill follows the house, not the seller. The closing office normally settles the current year's tax out of the seller's money, and the buyer carries it forward. Owners who let a bill go unpaid can face a tax foreclosure sale held at the courthouse door, with the sale price applied to taxes, penalties, interest and costs under G.S. 105-374.

For 2020 to 2024 Census data shows 80.6% owner-occupancy, a $446,200 median home value and $94,317 in median household income. Seniors make up 28.0% of the county, the group the exclusion and deferment programs are built for. Anyone receiving a program benefit should ask the Listing Division what a sale does to it.

What does recording a Chatham County deed cost?

North Carolina's excise tax of $1.00 per $500 of consideration is the seller's to pay at the register of deeds office, per G.S. 105-228.30. The Chatham County Register of Deeds charges $26.00 to record a deed of up to 15 pages and $4.00 for each additional page. A deed of trust runs $64 for up to 35 pages.

These recording amounts mirror the uniform schedule in G.S. 161-10. Your closing office will supply exact settlement figures, because they turn on the price and the number of pages.

More questions about Chatham County, NC Property Tax Guide

Where do I pay or question my Chatham County property tax bill?

Call the Tax Administration offices in Pittsboro. The Listing Division answers at 919-542-8250 and the Appraisal Division at 919-542-8211. Collections handles payments, and the Listing Division is at 12 East Street, open 8:00 to 5:00 on weekdays.

What is the Chatham County county-only tax rate?

The county-only rate on the 2026 rate sheet is 0.60, matching the 60 cents per $100 of valuation the commissioners kept for fiscal year 2026-27. Town and fire districts add their own rates, so the full rate turns on the parcel's location.

Is the 2026 appeal window still open?

No. The Board of Equalization and Review adjourned on April 20, 2026 at 5:00 p.m. and accepted no more appeals for tax year 2026. Owners can still talk to the Appraisal Division about errors, and the next reappraisal cycle brings a new notice and a new window.

Can a Chatham County senior get a lower assessment?

Yes, if income and age fit. The elderly or disabled exclusion removes the greater of $25,000 or 50% of a home's appraised value for owners 65 or older with income up to $38,800. File with the Tax Listing Office before June 1.

Who pays the deed excise tax in Chatham County?

The seller does. The statute puts the $1.00 per $500 charge on the transferor, payable to the register of deeds ahead of recording, and the closing office usually takes it from proceeds.

Cleveland County by the numbers

Which office bills and collects property tax in Cleveland County?

Cleveland County Tax Administration, in the county administration building at 311 East Marion Street in Shelby, appraises property and bills and collects the tax. The office phone is 704-484-4843, and its website says the doors are open from eight to five on weekdays.

The tax administrator's site describes a county of 469 square miles that includes 15 municipalities and says the office mails and collects more than 60,000 tax notices each fall. It offers a record lookup, an online payment search, an address change request and a tax estimator.

How often does Cleveland County revalue real property?

Cleveland County told owners it revalues on a four-year cycle, tighter than the eight-year ceiling in the statute. Its latest valuation date is January 1, 2025.

The county's revaluation page explains that values are set as of that date from aerial and street photography, recent sales, land records and details such as zoning, soil class and improvements. Owners received notices in mid-February 2025. An earlier revaluation took effect in 2021, and a county news release says the commissioners cut the rate from 57.0 cents per $100 to 54.75 cents afterward.

For a seller, that means the tax value on a Cleveland County parcel is pinned to January 1, 2025.

What rates make up a Cleveland County tax bill?

The County Manager's recommended 2026-2027 budget keeps the county rate at 40.5 cents per $100 of valuation. Added to a public school rate and a fire tax rate, the news release puts the total at 61.5 cents per $100.

Rates in the recommended Cleveland County fiscal year 2026-2027 budget, per $100 of valuation. Source: Cleveland County news release on the recommended budget.
ComponentRate as printed

Public school tax14 cents
Fire tax7 cents
Total61.5 cents

Confirm the adopted figures and any city or town rate with the tax office, because the release describes a recommended budget and a June public hearing. Ask the tax office which school, fire and municipal rates apply to your parcel.

How do I appeal a Cleveland County property value?

You can file a written appeal online, by mail or by email, or request an in-person meeting. Cleveland County does not accept an appeal by phone.

  • Online: use the appeal form on the county tax site, one form per parcel.
  • Mail: send a photocopy of the form to the Cleveland County Tax Assessor, P.O. Box 370, Shelby, NC 28151.
  • Email: tax.assessor@clevelandcountync.gov.
  • In person: complete the request form attached to your notice and call 704-484-4911 for an appointment.

Plan on at least eight weeks for a mailed decision, and note that a review can leave the value unchanged, lower it or raise it. The county accepts two reasons: the assessed value is well above market value, or the property was appraised unfairly compared with similar properties. It does not consider the size of the increase, an insurance value, a feeling that value is simply too high, or inability to pay.

Still unhappy after the informal review? Put a hearing request in writing to the Board of Equalization and Review before it adjourns; the county publishes the adjournment date in the local newspaper and on its site. The Property Tax Commission is the next stop, with a 30-day filing clock that starts when the board mails its ruling.

Does a higher appraisal always mean a higher Cleveland County tax bill?

No. The county's explanation is that a bill equals the tax value multiplied by the rate, and each taxing jurisdiction sets its own rate. After a revaluation some bills rise, some fall and some stay about the same.

The tax office says it can only act on the appraised value. Concerns about service levels or affordability belong with the elected boards that set rates, not with the appraisers. Before you appeal, open the county's assessment records map and turn on the Improved Sales and Vacant Sales layers, which the county recommends for finding recent comparable sales near your parcel. Personal property such as vehicles, trailers and boats is valued every year, while land and buildings are valued only at a countywide revaluation.

Which tax relief programs does Cleveland County offer?

The county tax assessor takes applications for three state programs. June 1 is the usual cutoff, and an owner may draw from just one program.

  • Elderly or disabled exclusion: $25,000 or half the home's appraised value, whichever is bigger, comes off the taxable amount. The 2026 income ceiling is $38,800.
  • Disabled veteran exclusion: $45,000 of appraised value is exempt, and the state form says no age or income test applies.
  • Circuit breaker: a 4 percent of income cap, or 5 percent for households between the limit and $58,200 in 2026. It requires five years of ownership and residence and a new application every year.

Deferred circuit breaker taxes for the prior three years come due if the home is transferred, so a sale ends the deferral and puts those taxes on the closing statement. The county also describes a present-use deferral for farm and forest land, which taxes at use value but keeps the deferred amount on the books.

What happens when a Cleveland County tax bill goes unpaid?

September 1 is the due date, with January 5 as the last interest-free day. The 2025 relief notice said bills would be calculated and mailed in July after the rate-setting boards act.

Interest of 2 percent attaches January 6, and three-fourths of 1 percent more builds each month from February 1. The lien is on the parcel from the listing date, which means an unpaid year stays with the house.

When a county forecloses for unpaid tax, the county's tax foreclosure page shows the process. Auctions take place in the Commissioners' Room, second floor, and the top bidder puts down 5 percent. A challenger must outbid by $750 or 5 percent, whichever is larger, filing in person at the courthouse, and every upset bid restarts a ten-day clock. Redemption by the owner stays open until the court confirms.

How is unpaid tax handled in a Cleveland County closing?

Ask the collector for a payoff figure, then have the settlement agent pay it out of the seller's proceeds so the buyer does not inherit it.

Past-due years are cleared at closing along with interest. If a parcel is already in foreclosure, the county's page says liens against it can be found in the complaint in the clerk's file, and you need the CV file number to pull it at the courthouse at 100 Justice Place in Shelby.

What do federal figures show for housing in Cleveland County?

The Census Bureau's QuickFacts shows 103,325 residents in July 2025 and 45,667 housing units. For 2020 to 2024, 70.9 percent of occupied homes are owner-held, the median value is $200,000, and median owner costs with a mortgage are $1,257 a month.

Rent has a median of $914, and the county recorded 555 permits in 2025. Persons in poverty make up 16.3 percent of the population.

More questions about Cleveland County, NC Property Tax Guide

When must a Cleveland County bill be paid?

By September 1; paying after January 5 adds 2 percent, then three-fourths of 1 percent for each month that follows beginning in February.

How do I challenge my Cleveland County appraisal?

File a written appeal online, by mail to P.O. Box 370, Shelby, or by email, or ask for an in-person appointment at 704-484-4911. The county does not take appeals by phone, and a mailed decision can take at least eight weeks.

Is Cleveland County on the standard eight-year cycle?

No. The statute caps the gap at eight years, but the county reports a four-year cycle, and its latest revaluation took effect January 1, 2025.

By when must relief paperwork reach the county?

The county sets June 1 as the usual deadline for the tax year. The elderly or disabled exclusion, disabled veteran exclusion and circuit breaker are all filed with the county, not the Department of Revenue.

May I close on a Cleveland County sale while taxes are owed?

Yes. Get the balance from the collector and have it paid out of your proceeds. If the county has started a foreclosure, you can still redeem until the court confirms the sale.

Where do Columbus County property tax bills get paid?

The Columbus County Tax Office collects at 810 Pinckney Street in Whiteville, and the public lobby keeps hours from half past eight to five The main tax office number is 910-640-6635, and the mailing address is P.O. Box 1468, Whiteville, NC 28472.

The county's collections page lists payment by mail, phone, online, dropbox or in person. Online payment runs through columbus.webtaxpay.com, and the phone line is 877-768-4775. Cash, check and credit card are all taken.

The collections page says the office collects for more than the county. It names the City of Whiteville and the towns of Fair Bluff, Sandyfield, Boardman, Brunswick, Cerro Gordo, Bolton, Chadbourn, Tabor City and Lake Waccamaw. For older years the page sends inquiries about some towns to the towns themselves, so call town hall if you cannot find an old balance.

What is the Columbus County property tax rate?

Columbus County sets $0.805 per $100 of assessed valuation for fiscal year 2026-2027, with all of it going to the General Fund. Commissioners adopted the budget ordinance on June 1, 2026.

The ordinance bases that rate on an estimated total valuation of $4,010,748,958 and a collection rate of 97.72 percent, and it says discounts will be allowed for early payment. Public schools are funded through two systems, Columbus County Schools and Whiteville City Schools. The ordinance also levies a special fire tax by district on top of the county rate.

Ask the tax office which fire district a given parcel sits in, and whether a city or town levy applies as well.

When did Columbus County last revalue, and when is the next one?

The last revaluation was in 2021, and the county's budget message to commissioners in May 2026 says the next one is not until 2029.

The same message explains why that timing matters. It says property tax revenue stays relatively flat except in revaluation years and that the county collects roughly $30 million a year. A seller in Columbus County is therefore likely to see an assessed value that was set in 2021. The Census Bureau's median owner-occupied value for 2020 to 2024 is $146,000; ask the appraisal staff how your parcel was valued if your own figure looks far from that.

What are the Columbus County payment deadlines and late charges?

Payment is due September 1, and January 5 is the last day before delinquency. The county's collections page says amounts are good through the last day of the month and that interest of three-fourths of 1 percent accrues on the first day of each month on delinquent taxes.

State law adds a 2 percent charge from January 6 to February 1, under G.S. 105-360. Mailed payments count as received on the USPS postmark date.

Once a parcel has been advertised for sale, only certified funds are accepted to redeem it. The county's page says that once a sale is confirmed by the court there is no redemption in North Carolina. To find out whether a property is in tax foreclosure proceedings, the tax collector's office invites you to contact it directly.

How does a tax foreclosure sale work in Columbus County?

Sales are held outside the main entrance of the Columbus County Courthouse unless the weather is bad. The county's foreclosures page says the notice posted at the courthouse and printed in the newspaper controls, and the page itself is only an informal list of answers.

  • The high bidder must pay a deposit of 20 percent of the bid or $750, whichever is greater. On sales over $5,000 a $1,000 cash deposit is due immediately, with the rest within two business days.
  • Every bid is open to a 10-day upset period, and upset bids are filed through the Clerk of Court with a 5 percent or $750 deposit, whichever is greater.
  • After the upset period ends and the sale is confirmed, the last high bidder has three days to pay the balance to the commissioner.
  • The owner keeps the property until a new deed is recorded and may redeem it until the court confirms the sale.

Upset bid amounts are found through the NC eCourts portal with the full file number, and the form to bid is AOC-CV-414. The clerk will not answer upset bid questions by phone or fill out the form for you.

What property tax relief does Columbus County offer?

The county posts an application for the elderly and disabled exclusion, and the state also offers a disabled veteran exclusion and a circuit breaker deferral. Filing opens January 1 and closes June 1, and one program per owner is the limit.

  • County application page (2025 tax year): household income at or under $37,900, status as 65 or older or permanently and totally disabled on January 1, and a permanent residence titled in the applicant's exact name.
  • State figures for the 2026 tax year: the income ceiling rises to $38,800, and the amount excluded is whichever is bigger, $25,000 or half the appraised value.
  • Disabled veterans: $45,000 of appraised value is excluded, with no age or income test, using Form NCDVA-9.
  • Circuit breaker: tax limited to 4 percent of income up to the limit, 5 percent above it up to 150 percent of the limit.

The county asks for the prior year's income tax statement, an SSA-1099, a doctor's certification for applicants under 65 and a death certificate where a spouse has died and the deed was not corrected. It says applications are denied if they are incomplete, if the name on the deed does not match the application or if they miss the deadline. The county notes that an approved elderly or disabled application does not have to be repeated every year unless household circumstances or income change; the state says a circuit breaker application is filed anew each year.

How do I appeal a Columbus County assessment?

Talk to the appraisal staff first; if that fails, the next forum is the county's equalization board. State law makes the commissioners that board unless a special one is created, so ask who sits on Columbus County's.

The board opens its session between the first Monday in April and the first Monday in May. In an ordinary year it wraps up by the third Monday after that first meeting and generally cannot sit beyond July 1. A hearing request, in writing or in person, must arrive before adjournment, or within 15 days of a late-mailed notice. Rulings are mailed within 30 days.

Beyond that sits the Property Tax Commission, which has a 30-day filing window running from the board's mailing date. Personal property such as vehicles and equipment is handled by separate staff at the tax office.

What else is on a Columbus County title search that affects a sale?

The county tax office page reproduces a state notice, Session Law 2018-113 and G.S. 106-741, about farm proximity. Land records must carry a notice alerting a person researching title that a tract lies within one-half mile of a poultry, swine or dairy qualifying farm or a voluntary agricultural district, or within 600 feet of any other qualifying farm.

The same page lists staff for the solid waste trash user fee and for senior citizen exemptions, so ask the tax office whether any trash fee is attached to a parcel before closing. Columbus County covers 938.12 square miles of land with about 54 people per square mile, so farm and rural parcels are common and the notice is worth reading.

What is the Columbus County housing stock like?

The Census Bureau's QuickFacts estimates 50,487 residents for July 2025 and 23,724 housing units. Population was 58,098 in 2010 and 50,623 in 2020.

Homeowners occupy 71.1 percent of housing, valued at a median $146,000, while renters pay a median gross $824 (2020 to 2024). A typical household earns $49,442 a year, and the poverty rate is 19.3 percent. Only 55 building permits were issued in 2025, and veterans number 2,668.

What is the Columbus County property tax rate?

The adopted fiscal year 2026-2027 county rate is $0.805 per $100 of assessed value. Fire district taxes range from 0.06 to 0.12 per $100, and city or town taxes are billed separately.

When are Columbus County property taxes due?

September 1 is the due date, and January 5 is the last day to pay before interest begins, which then builds at three-fourths of 1 percent a month after the initial January 6 charge.

Where do I pay Columbus County property taxes in person?

Pay at the Columbus County Tax Office, 810 Pinckney Street, Whiteville. Staff serve the public lobby from half past eight until five, and you can also pay by mail, by phone at 877-768-4775, online or at the dropbox.

When is the next Columbus County revaluation?

The county's May 2026 budget message says the next revaluation is not until 2029. The previous revaluation was in 2021.

Can I stop a Columbus County tax foreclosure?

An owner can redeem until the court confirms the sale, by paying the taxes, interest and costs. After advertising, the county takes certified funds only.

Who bills and assesses property tax in Craven County, NC?

The Craven County Tax Administration at 226 Pollock Street in New Bern handles both jobs: it appraises real estate and it collects the bills. The counter is staffed from eight in the morning until five on weekdays. Appraisal questions go to the real estate appraisal division at 252-636-6640.

The department also runs separate divisions for tax collection (252-636-6605), business personal property and non-business personal property. Motor vehicle tax follows its own tag-and-tax system through the state, and the department's menu covers gap bills for vehicles, so a house seller can ignore those unless a closing statement mentions one.

The county site names eight municipalities: Bridgeton, Cove City, Dover, Havelock, New Bern, River Bend, Trent Woods and Vanceboro. Land area totals 706.57 square miles, and the Census Bureau's July 2025 estimate shows 105,025 residents.

What is the Craven County property tax rate?

With its 2026-2027 budget, the board of commissioners held the rate at 44.48 cents per $100 of assessed value. That figure is the county's own levy. Confirm any town or district charge stacked on it using the 2026 tax rates document on the county site.

Rates apply to assessed value after any exclusion you have been granted. The state exclusions come in three kinds. Under the elderly or disabled exclusion, the larger of $25,000 or 50% of a permanent residence's appraised value is set aside, and the 2026 income limit is $38,800. A disabled veteran has the first $45,000 of appraised value excluded, with no age or income test. The circuit breaker limits the bill to 4.0% of income, or 5.0% for income above that limit but within 150% of it; NCDOR prints that upper figure as $58,200 for 2026.

Value and rate come from different decisions. The county's revaluation FAQ explains that a revaluation sets market value, while the commissioners set the rate for budget needs. A higher assessment therefore does not by itself mean a higher rate, and a held rate can still produce a larger bill when the value goes up.

The county's tax menu has a page for each program. Owners apply on Form AV-9 at the assessor's office, and the county must take one up to June 1 of the preceding year.

What dates matter on a Craven County tax bill?

Billing opens September 1 and interest-free payment ends January 5. The collection division's list of dates is condensed below.

Under G.S. 105-360, interest opens at 2% on January 6 and climbs three-fourths of one percent for every month or fraction beginning February 1.

How do I pay a Craven County property tax bill?

  • Online at my.cravencountync.gov. A lookup by name, address or parcel number leads to the bill, and the platform allows scheduled and partial payments.
  • By mail to Craven County Tax Collector, PO Box 1128, New Bern, NC 28563-1128.
  • At the counter, 226 Pollock Street, with check, cash, money order or card, or in the drop box at the front right of the building. Cash does not belong in the drop box.

The county page for online payments points to a payment vendor for help, and the tax menu lists pre-payments and a delinquent payment assistance page. For delinquent bills, the county refers owners to NCHomeownerAssistance.gov and the state hotline 1-855-696-2423.

Before a sale, request a payoff amount covering this year and any unpaid earlier years. A lien for real property tax attaches to the parcel as of its listing date (G.S. 105-355), which is why a payoff letter protects both sides.

When did Craven County last revalue property, and when is the next time?

Tax year 2023 carried the most recent revaluation, and tax year 2028 is next. Notices of new value went out the week of February 27, 2023, and appeals were due by 5:00 p.m. on May 22, 2023.

Before that, Craven County's last revaluation was 2016. The commissioners had shortened the cycle to six years in 2011 and to four years after 2016, but Hurricane Florence in 2018 caused the planned 2020 revaluation to slip to 2023. G.S. 105-286 sets eight years as the longest gap. Counties of 75,000 or more can be pushed into an earlier cycle when sales assessment ratios drift under .85 or over 1.15, and Craven says its population falls in that group.

A Revaluation 2028 page already exists, and its comparable-sales search tool is marked "coming February 2028." Values are set as market value on January 1 of the revaluation year.

How do I appeal a Craven County property value?

File a signed appeal form with the county assessor ahead of the date printed on your notice. For the 2023 revaluation the county set that deadline at the board's adjournment date, May 22, 2023.

  • Attach comparable sales dated on or before January 1 of the revaluation year, photos of the property's condition, and a recent appraisal or market analysis if you have one.
  • The owner, an attorney or an agent under power of attorney can sign. A close family member may also appear when the owner cannot, such as during unexpected military duty or a hospital stay.
  • An appraiser reviews your file and mails a result that may raise the value, cut it or leave it alone.
  • If you still disagree, the Board of Equalization and Review takes the case, with a hearing letter sent at least 15 days ahead.
  • Bring copies of your evidence for the seven board members.

The Property Tax Commission is the next stop after the board. Written notice must be filed within 30 days of the board's mailing date, and the assessor gets a copy (G.S. 105-290).

What do Census figures say about Craven County homes?

Census estimates for 2020-2024 put the middle owner-occupied home at $231,600, and owners live in 68.4% of homes. Household income has a median of $65,873, and gross rent a median of $1,110 monthly.

Residents 65 or older make up 24.2% of the population, so the elderly exclusion and circuit breaker matter to many owners. The county counts 50,334 housing units, issued 553 building permits in 2025, and has 10,968 veterans, so the disabled veteran exclusion also reaches a meaningful number of owners.

Other items on the county's tax menu that can change a bill or a listing:

  • A Present Use Value Exclusion page.
  • Historic Properties, Builders Exclusion, Religious Uses Exemption and Antique Airplane and Automobile Exclusion pages.

  • Change of mailing address forms, so a seller's final bill reaches the right place after closing.

Delinquency begins January 6. Notices follow in mid-January, setoff notices and garnishment steps in mid-February, and a newspaper list appears after March 31.

What are the Cumberland County property tax rates?

On 2026 bills (fiscal year 2027) the county's general rate is 49.9 cents per $100 of valuation, and a 5.0-cent special recreation rate is listed beside it. Towns levy their own rates as well, so a parcel's total depends on its location.

The page also lists Wade, Falcon, Godwin, Linden, a Vander district and a Fayetteville Revitalization District with an added 0.1489 levy. The county notes that combined rates exclude storm water, solid waste, refuse, recycling and transit and auto privilege charges.

What flat fees show up on a Cumberland County tax bill?

Several service charges appear on the same bill and sit outside the rate. The county prints these amounts:

  • Solid waste fee of $285 a year for Fayetteville residences with seven or fewer units.
  • Solid waste fee of $130 a year for unincorporated areas and all municipalities except Spring Lake.
  • Refuse tax of $342.72 a year in Hope Mills and $396.00 in Spring Lake, the latter including a $12 residential litter control fee.
  • Fayetteville residential storm water by impervious surface: $84.00 below 2,500 square feet, $168.00 for 2,501 to 4,800, $252.00 beyond that.
  • Residential storm water of $60 a year in Spring Lake and in Hope Mills.
  • Vehicle fees: $25 vehicle fee plus a $5 transit tax in Fayetteville, $10 in Hope Mills, and $5 each in Stedman and Spring Lake.

When you compare a sale offer against your annual carrying cost, look at the bill line by line rather than the rate alone. A move across a town line can change the charges more than the home's value would.

When are Cumberland County taxes due, and what if I am late?

The county's 2026 rate page says bills are due September 1 and need to be paid by January 5 to escape interest, penalties and collection.

After that the statute (G.S. 105-360) charges 2% starting January 6, then three-fourths of one percent for each month or fraction from February 1. MyCCNCPay accepts credit, debit or electronic draft payments, and the same phone number above arranges a payment plan.

The annual listing period for property closes January 31 under G.S. 105-307, and the county posted a reminder of that deadline on January 15, 2026.

Unpaid bills can end in a tax foreclosure sale, which an outside attorney runs for the tax office. The county's foreclosure page names that attorney, and that office has sale dates and parcels in an upset bid period. An owner can still redeem by paying taxes, penalties, interest and costs before the court confirms the sale (G.S. 105-374).

How did the 2025 revaluation work in Cumberland County?

Real property was reappraised countywide for 2025, eight years after the January 1, 2017 revaluation. The county calls this an eight-year cycle, matching G.S. 105-286.

  • February 21, 2025: notices mailed to owners.
  • March 24, 2025: deadline for an informal appeal to Tax Administration.
  • April 23, 2025: Board of Equalization and Review convened.
  • May 28, 2025: deadline for a formal appeal, and the board adjourned.
  • July 1, 2025: new rates using the updated values took effect, with bills mailed that August.

Owners who agreed with the notice did not need to respond. The notice carried an informal appeal form on its back, assessed values were posted online from February 24, 2025, and a Revaluation Call Center at 910-678-7800 booked appointments with appraisers. The county urged owners to review three state relief programs at the same time: present use deferment, the elderly or disabled exclusion and the disabled veteran exclusion.

Those dates are history now. The pattern repeats each year in a smaller form: the board convened April 22, 2026, accepted real property appeals until its adjournment on May 20, and set hearings by letter.

How do I appeal a Cumberland County assessment?

Start with an informal review, then send a formal request to the Board of Equalization and Review before it adjourns. Delivery options: Room 543 of the courthouse, PO Box 449 in Fayetteville (ZIP 28302), or the secure drop box on the courthouse's rear lot.

Requests must be in writing. An appraiser contacts every taxpayer who appeals, and a letter gives the hearing date and time if the case proceeds to the board. The county suggests appraisals, comparable properties, income and expense statements, repair cost estimates and photos of unusual conditions as evidence.

The regular board's first meeting falls between the first Monday in April and the first Monday in May. Outside a revaluation year it wraps up by the third Monday after starting, unless it needs longer, and cannot sit past July 1. A special board meets at 3:30 p.m. on the second Wednesday of each month except July and approves corrections, clerical errors included. A board decision can be taken to the state Property Tax Commission within 30 days of the notice's mailing (G.S. 105-290).

What do Census figures say about selling a house in Cumberland County?

Owners occupy 55.0% of homes, which leaves about 45% to renters, so rental property is a large part of the market. For 2020-2024 the middle owner-occupied home is valued at $199,200, household income is $61,291 and gross rent is $1,222 a month.

  • Housing units, July 2025: 146,623.
  • Households, 2020-2024: 129,758.
  • Veterans: 40,226.
  • Residents 65 and older: 15.0%.
  • Building permits issued in 2025: 1,547.
  • Mean commute to work: 21.6 minutes.

With 40,226 veterans, the disabled veteran exclusion is worth a check. That program excludes the first $45,000 of appraised value, with no age or income test, using Form NCDVA-9 that a Veterans Service Officer completes first. Elderly or disabled relief and the circuit breaker go through Form AV-9 at the assessor, accepted up to June 1.

More questions about Cumberland County, NC Property Tax Guide

When are Cumberland County property taxes due?

Every September 1, with January 5 as the last day before interest. The 2% charge starts January 6.

What is the combined rate inside Fayetteville city limits?

The county lists the City of Fayetteville municipal rate at 0.4495 and the county rate at 0.499, for a combined 0.9485 per $100 on 2026 bills.

Where does a formal appeal go?

Take it to Room 543 of the courthouse, mail it to PO Box 449, or use the secure drop box. It must be in writing and in hand before the board adjourns.

When was the last Cumberland County revaluation?

The 2025 revaluation is the latest, with notices mailed February 21, 2025. The one before it was effective January 1, 2017.

Who runs Cumberland County tax foreclosure sales?

An outside attorney conducts them on behalf of the Tax Office. Call the attorney's office listed on the county's foreclosure page for sale dates and upset bid status.

Davidson County by the numbers

Which Davidson County offices bill and value property?

Davidson County runs its property tax through a Tax Assessor side that lists and values property and a Tax Collector side that bills and collects. Both are found at 913 Greensboro Street, 3rd Floor, Suite 303, in Lexington (NC 27292), open weekdays from 8:00 AM to 5:00 PM. A second counter in Denton opens at 8:30 AM on weekdays.

  • Tax office and appeals line: 336-242-2160.
  • Collections line: 336-242-2180.
  • Mailing address for the assessor: P.O. Box 1617, Lexington, NC 27293.
  • Mailing address for payments: Davidson County Tax Collector, P.O. Box 1577, Lexington, NC 27293.

The county's Collections page says questions about listing, billing and assessed values go to the assessor's side, while the collector is responsible only for collecting what is owed.

What are the 2026 Davidson County tax rates?

The county's own line reads 0.5400 on the 2026 sheet, and a parcel inside a city, school district or fire district picks up that jurisdiction's line too. The sheet carries the word tentative in its heading, so verify the adopted numbers with the tax office.

Fire district rates are listed separately and run from 0.0965 for Reeds Fire to 0.1624 for Healing Springs Fire. City motor vehicle fees are $30.00 in Lexington and High Point, $20.00 in Thomasville and $5.00 in Denton, and the Lexington sheet notes that discounts are not applied to the city and municipal service district lines.

When are Davidson County property tax bills due?

Bills for land, buildings and business or personal items are mailed each July. They fall due September 1 and carry no interest until after January 5. A weekend January 5 pushes the deadline to the following business day.

The county gives a 1 1/2 percent discount for payment in July and a 1 percent discount in August. A January 5 postmark counts as timely, though the county advises mailing a full week early. Past-due real estate accounts are charged 2 percent for January and an extra 3/4 percent each month after that, which matches the state schedule. Payment plans have to be arranged when the annual bill arrives and finished by the delinquent date, and card payments are taken at the office.

What is happening with the Davidson County revaluation?

Davidson County's last revaluation took effect January 1, 2021, and the county's pages say the planned 2026 revaluation was postponed until 2027 under new legislation. State law requires counties to reappraise at least once every eight years, and the county reviews more than 97,000 parcels in a revaluation.

The county explains that revaluation is meant to equalize values, not raise revenue, and that tax rates are set by elected officials in June. Owners who appealed their 2026 or 2027 values on time do not need to refile, and any change from those appeals will apply to the 2027 tax year. The informal appeal deadline for the 2026 round was 5:00 PM on Thursday, April 30, 2026, and it has passed. The county's appeal page offers separate forms for the current 2026 value and the 2027 revaluation value, and the revaluation help address is revalhelp@davidsoncountync.gov.

What steps does a Davidson County owner follow to contest a value?

Appeals have three levels, and the first is an informal review with a county appraiser, who looks at your property record and any supporting evidence with you. If an error turns up, it can be fixed without a formal appeal.

The second step is a formal hearing at the county's Board of Equalization and Review. Under state law the commissioners sit as that board unless a special one is created; Davidson County describes its board as local residents with real estate knowledge, appointed by the commissioners. A written notice to the state Property Tax Commission is the step after an unwelcome board decision. The county lists reasons that do not count as grounds:

  • The size of the percentage increase or decrease.
  • A market value above the insurance value.
  • A feeling that the value is simply too high.
  • An owner's inability to pay the tax.

Which property tax relief programs can a Davidson County owner use?

State law sets up three homestead programs and lets each owner use just one. The first program, for older or disabled owners, excludes whichever is bigger: $25,000 or half the appraised value. Qualifying means being 65 or older, or disabled for good, and earning no more than $38,800 for 2026.

The circuit breaker is the second: it holds the bill to 4.0 percent of income for owners at or below the limit, and to 5.0 percent for owners whose income reaches 150 percent of it ($58,200 for 2026). Five years of owning and occupying the home come first. The third takes $45,000 off the value for a disabled veteran with no age or income test. Form AV-9 goes to the county assessor, and the county's property information page links to the homestead application. Any tax deferred under the circuit breaker turns into a lien and becomes payable when the property transfers, which matters at a sale.

What happens to unpaid Davidson County property tax?

Interest starts on a bill after the January 5 deadline, and after that the bill is subject to collection actions. The collector lists wage garnishment, attachment of bank accounts or rents, levy on personal property and, for real estate, tax foreclosure by sale at public auction.

  • Unpaid real estate accounts can be advertised in local newspapers from March 1 to June 30, at added cost to the taxpayer.
  • The county also lists sheriff's warrants, in rem foreclosures and attachment of the state tax refund.
  • State law sets the lien date as the listing date, so the lien exists before the bill is due.

The county posts a PDF list of 2025 delinquent taxpayers and a tax foreclosure list. If a sale is pending, Davidson County also requires a tax certificate before the Register of Deeds takes a deed, so a delinquent balance has to be cleared first.

What does the Census count in Davidson County?

The Census estimate for July 2025 is 180,182 residents, and the five-year survey counts 69,846 households, 74.4 percent of them owning. The median owned home is valued at $219,100. Monthly costs for owners carrying a mortgage come to $1,355 at the median, and the median household brings in $64,172 (2024 dollars).

The county's rate sheet lists Lexington, Thomasville, Denton, Wallburg, Midway and High Point as taxing cities and towns, along with two school districts and dozens of fire districts. Ask the tax office which of those lines apply to your parcel.

How should I handle taxes when I sell a Davidson County house?

Ask whether the seller's share of the current bill is prorated at closing, and if you want zero exposure, have the closing attorney pay the collector from the proceeds. Per the county, selling during the year does not release the January 1 owner from that year's bill.

Request a tax certificate early if no attorney is closing. Check the 2026 or 2027 appeal status too, because a value change from an appeal lands in the 2027 tax year.

More questions about Davidson County, NC Property Tax Guide

When are Davidson County property taxes due?

Payment is due September 1, with no interest through January 5. July payments earn a 1 1/2 percent discount and August payments earn 1 percent.

What is the Davidson County tax rate?

County-only is 0.5400 on the 2026 sheet, and cities, schools and fire districts add their own rates. Lexington is printed at 0.6500 and Thomasville at 0.6200, and the sheet is marked tentative, so confirm final rates with the tax office.

Was the Davidson County revaluation postponed?

Yes. The county says its 2026 revaluation was postponed until 2027 under new legislation. Appeals filed on time for 2026 or 2027 values still get reviewed, and any change applies to the 2027 tax year.

How can I contest my Davidson County property value?

Start by filing the county's form for an informal sit-down with an appraiser. Only if that falls short does the matter go on to a formal hearing. The state Property Tax Commission hears later appeals, and the 30 days run from the board's mailing date.

What interest applies to late Davidson County taxes?

Past-due real estate accounts are charged 2 percent for January and 3/4 percent for each month after that. The county urges mailing payments at least five business days before the January 5 deadline.

Davie County by the numbers

Which Davie County offices handle property tax?

Davie County Tax Administration splits the work into three divisions: real property appraisal (which includes mapping and land records), personal property appraisal, and tax collection. Billing and payment sit with the collector, and anything about a listing or an assessed value goes to the assessor.

Listings are taken at the Administration Building, 123 South Main Street, Mocksville, on weekdays between 8 AM and 5 PM, in person, online or by mail. The assessor's line is 336 753-6120 and the revaluation staff take calls at 336-753-6140. Real property appeals go to the same street address.

If you are thinking about selling a Davie County house, call the collector first for a current balance on the parcel, then call the assessor if the value or an exemption looks wrong on the card.

What does Davie County look like for a home seller?

Davie County is a mostly rural county in the Piedmont Triad that is gaining suburban residents. The county's own profile names Mocksville as the county seat and largest town (over 5,000 people, incorporated 1839), Cooleemee (over 950, incorporated 1985) and Bermuda Run (over 2,500, incorporated 1999).

Outside those three towns, the county lists unincorporated communities such as Advance, Farmington, Fulton, Cornatzer, Smith Grove, Jerusalem and Shady Grove. Davie sits on a corridor served by I-40, I-85 and I-77.

Here is what Census QuickFacts shows for Davie:

  • A July 2025 estimate of 45,855 people, a 7.3% rise over the 42,719 counted in the April 2020 base.
  • Land area of 263.70 square miles, with a 2020 density of 162.0 people per square mile.
  • 82.2% owner-occupied housing, with a median owner-occupied value of $253,900 for 2020-2024.
  • Median household income of $75,057 and median gross rent of $867.
  • Building permits totaled 236 in 2025, and 24.2% of residents are 65 or older.

The exclusions covered below attach to an owner's permanent residence, so they matter in a county where 82.2% of housing is owner-occupied.

What are the Davie County tax rates for 2026-27?

Davie County lists a countywide rate of $0.6486 per $100 of valuation for the 2026-2027 fiscal year, with extra layers depending on where the parcel sits. The commissioners and town boards usually adopt rates in June, and the county explains a bill as tax value multiplied by the rate.

AreaRate as printed
